I will start from what has worked on my land and then adjust a little, not too much. I have 13.1 mu and well water, so I do not farm like a man waiting only on the sky. I have been doing this 30 years, and with my education I look at it in terms of yield, fertilizer response, and labor. Wheat-maize is still my main steady income because on irrigated land here in Quzhou County it is the safest way to keep grain coming. Cotton can still make money, but it takes more watching, more pesticide, and more hand labor at the wrong time, so I will not let cotton take too much of the land. I will keep 8.0 mu in the wheat-maize rotation and 5.1 mu in cotton. That way I spread risk: grain for stability, cotton for cash.

For wheat, I will go a bit heavier on nitrogen than a low-input household because if wheat is short of fertilizer in spring, yield loss is hard to recover. I will still keep phosphorus in because our land responds better when the base fertilizer is balanced, and I will not ignore potassium completely even if some people around here try to save that money. I will irrigate three times if water and weather allow: one good winter or overwintering water if needed, one at jointing, and one at grain filling depending on moisture. After wheat harvest, I will put summer maize on that same 8.0 mu. Maize on irrigated land can carry good yield if I keep population, fertilizer, and one or two timely irrigations. I will use hybrid maize because that is standard now and the return is there. For cotton, I will stay more conservative on area but not on management. Cotton needs steady feeding and more pest watching, especially later in the season. I will put more potassium there than on grain because cotton uses it well, and I will spray more times than wheat or maize because if insects get ahead, picking suffers and the whole field looks weak. I would rather spend some extra yuan on fertilizer and one more spray than lose yield on 13.1 mu.

decision.reasoning_summary: I will keep 8.0 mu in the wheat-maize rotation and 5.1 mu in cotton because irrigated wheat-maize is my steady base and cotton is the higher-management cash crop. On wheat and maize I will aim for stable grain output with balanced nitrogen, phosphorus, and some potassium; on cotton I will put relatively more potassium and more pesticide sprays because cotton is more sensitive to late-season stress and insects.
